<meta>continues from previous page</meta>What then, or in what way, does God foreknow these uncertain future events? For if He judges that future things are avoidable <note>original: "evitabilia"</note>, it is not possible for those things to happen. If so, He is deceived, and it is a wicked thing not only to feel this but even to speak it. 

But if He discerns that these future events will occur exactly as they are, so that He knows they are able either to happen or not to happen, what kind of foreknowledge is this, which grasps nothing certain and nothing stable? Or how does this differ from that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias <note>A blind prophet of Thebes in Greek mythology</note>, who said: Whatever I say will either happen or it will not? 

Furthermore, how would divine providence differ from human opinion if, like humans, He judges uncertain things whose outcome is unsure? But if nothing uncertain can exist for that most certain fountain of all things <note>referring to the divine mind as the source of all knowledge</note>

<summary>Boethius questions how God can have certain knowledge of future events that are inherently uncertain and avoidable. He argues that if divine foreknowledge is not absolute, it would be no better than human guesswork or the ambiguous prophecies of Tiresias.</summary>
<keywords>divine foreknowledge, free will, Tiresias, providence, certainty, divine mind, future contingents</keywords>
